stories.headline: Radar pass by hurricane hunter gives officials first look at Rafael flooding in Corpus Christi
stories.dek: A NOAA aircraft imaged Corpus Christi Bay and the ship channel about two and a half hours after landfall, before ground crews could safely move.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Before any ground crew could safely reach the flooded edges of this port city Tuesday, federal and state emergency managers already had a picture of it. A NOAA Hurricane Hunter aircraft made a final reconnaissance pass over the Corpus Christi area at about 3:30 a.m. CDT, roughly two and a half hours after Hurricane Rafael came ashore, and captured radar imagery of Corpus Christi Bay and the ship channel, the National Hurricane Center said.

The imagery is synthetic aperture radar, a sensor that sees through cloud, rain and darkness. According to the hurricane center, it shows the extent of storm surge flooding along the ship channel's industrial corridor and in coastal residential areas of the city, and it is now available to federal and state emergency managers. It will also be shared with FEMA Region 6 and the Texas General Land Office for use in assessing damage to infrastructure.

State officials described the pass as a way to buy time. The Texas Division of Emergency Management said the imagery gives coordinating agencies a first look at how far the water reached before ground teams can safely enter, and called it a critical input to initial damage estimates and to decisions about where search and rescue crews go first.

That ordering problem is the central one in the first hours after a major landfall. Roads are blocked or under water, the wind is still too strong for most aircraft, and the people who most need help are often in the places that are hardest to see. Radar collected from above the storm lets planners mark which neighborhoods are likely under water and which routes may be passable, without waiting for daylight or calmer air.

The imagery has not been released to the public, and officials gave no damage figures Tuesday morning. A radar picture of standing water is not a count of damaged homes or of people in danger; those numbers come later, from crews on the ground and from follow-up surveys.

Rafael made landfall on Mustang Island near Port Aransas about 1 a.m. Tuesday as a Category 3 hurricane. An emergency alert issued shortly before landfall told everyone who had not evacuated to shelter in place, and officials said Tuesday morning that the instruction still stands.

stories.headline: Seven times the calls, the same number of chairs: inside the first hours at the 911 center
stories.dek: The Coastal Bend's dispatch hub is at maximum surge capacity and borrowing dispatchers from two neighboring counties. What that means for someone waiting on the line.
body: Somewhere in Corpus Christi this morning, a person is holding a phone and listening to it ring. The wind has dropped enough to hear the water moving in the street. The call will be answered, emergency officials say. The question on a morning like this is how long it takes, and who else is in line.

The Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center, the 911 dispatch hub for Nueces County, said Tuesday morning that it is operating at maximum surge capacity as Hurricane Rafael moves inland. Director Patricia Escamilla-Voss said the center is receiving approximately seven times its normal call volume and has activated mutual aid with the dispatch centers in San Patricio and Bee counties.

"Our dispatchers are working alongside mutual aid partners to answer every call as quickly as possible," Escamilla-Voss said. "Please call 911 only for immediate life-safety emergencies. We need to keep the lines open for people in immediate danger."

Mutual aid is the system's pressure valve. A 911 center is built for an ordinary day, with a fixed number of consoles and people trained to work them. When calls multiply, neighboring centers take the overflow, answering as if they were in the same room and passing each emergency to the units that can reach it. It adds hands. It does not add boats, helicopters or passable roads, and during the height of a hurricane crews cannot always be sent, however fast the phone is answered.

That is why officials are asking people to sort their own calls. The center urged residents to shelter in place if it is safe to do so and not to call 911 for flooding updates that do not involve a person in immediate danger. People with non-emergency needs were asked to wait until the storm has passed and to check the City of Corpus Christi website and social media for road closures, shelters and power outages.

The burden of that advice does not fall evenly. A household with a car, a charged phone and a second floor can wait for information. A household in a one-story rental near the bay, with water coming in, cannot. The center has not said where today's calls are coming from. After past storms on this coast, the heaviest need has come from low-lying neighborhoods where fewer people had a way to leave.
If you must call: say where you are first, then how many people are with you and whether anyone is hurt. If the water is rising, move to the highest floor you can reach.

stories.headline: How do you map a flood you can't reach? Radar from a plane, then radar from space
stories.dek: Two kinds of imagery, one from a hurricane hunter and one from satellites, are telling responders where Rafael's water went. Here is what each can and cannot show.
body: On a radar image, calm floodwater looks like spilled ink. Streets, yards and parking lots that should scatter a signal back toward the sensor instead go dark, and the dark shape is the flood. That is the picture emergency managers have been working from since before sunrise Tuesday, when most of the places in it could not be reached by road.

The first image came from the air. The National Hurricane Center said a NOAA Hurricane Hunter aircraft made a final pass over the Corpus Christi area at about 3:30 a.m. Tuesday, roughly two and a half hours after Hurricane Rafael made landfall, and collected synthetic aperture radar imagery of Corpus Christi Bay and the ship channel. The center said the imagery shows the extent of surge flooding along the ship channel's industrial corridor and in coastal residential areas, and that it has been given to federal and state emergency managers, with copies going to FEMA Region 6 and the Texas General Land Office.

The second came from orbit. Satellite imagery analyzed Wednesday shows about 43 square miles flooded across Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties. The two sources answer different questions. The aircraft pass is early and close: it covers the bay and the channel within hours of landfall. The satellite view is wide: it takes in all three counties at once.

What neither can do is count. Radar shows where water is standing at the moment the sensor passes over. It does not show how deep the water is inside a house, whether anyone is in that house, or what the wind did to the roof. The Texas Division of Emergency Management described the aircraft imagery as a first look before ground teams can safely enter, and as an input to initial damage estimates and to setting priorities for search and rescue. An input is not an answer.

It matters who is inside the dark shapes. Much of the low ground near the bay and along the channel is home to renters, older residents and households without a car, the same neighborhoods where county officials urged people before the storm to sign up for evacuation rides. A flood map tells responders where to look first. It will take people on the ground, going door to door, to learn who was there.
Officials have not released the radar imagery itself. They say more detailed surveys, flown lower and slower once the weather allows, will follow in the coming days.

stories.headline: El 9-1-1 recibe casi diez veces más llamadas de lo normal: cuándo llamar y qué decir / 911 is taking nearly ten times its normal calls: when to call and what to say
stories.dek: El centro de despacho trabaja con ayuda de dos condados vecinos. Reserve el 9-1-1 para emergencias de vida o muerte. / The dispatch center is working with help from two neighboring counties; keep 911 for life-threatening emergencies.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas — Un día después de que el huracán Rafael tocó tierra, el centro de llamadas de emergencia del condado sigue saturado. Las llamadas al 9-1-1 están llegando a un ritmo de cerca de 2,900 al día, casi diez veces lo normal, y la mayoría viene de los barrios bajos cerca de la bahía, informaron las autoridades este miércoles.

El Centro de Comunicaciones de Emergencia del Coastal Bend, que atiende el 9-1-1 para el condado de Nueces, trabaja a su máxima capacidad con el apoyo de despachadores de los condados de San Patricio y Bee. "Nuestros despachadores trabajan junto con nuestros socios de ayuda mutua para contestar cada llamada lo más rápido posible", dijo la directora del centro, Patricia Escamilla-Voss, en declaraciones traducidas por KNCB.
Cuándo llamar al 9-1-1: si alguien está en peligro inmediato. Si el agua sigue subiendo dentro de su casa, si hay una persona herida, atrapada o que no puede respirar, llame.

Cuándo no llamar: para preguntar por inundaciones, calles cerradas, albergues o cuándo vuelve la luz. Para esa información, el centro pide consultar la página y las redes sociales de la ciudad de Corpus Christi.

Qué decir cuando le contesten: primero su dirección o el cruce de calles más cercano. Después, cuántas personas hay y si alguien está herido. Hable despacio, repita la dirección y no cuelgue hasta que se lo indiquen.
Mientras espera ayuda: suba al piso más alto que pueda. Use una linterna o el teléfono para hacer señales desde una ventana. No camine ni maneje por el agua.
El puente Harbor y la calzada de la bahía de Nueces siguen cerrados, y Portland y North Beach están aislados del centro hasta que terminen las inspecciones.

In English: 911 calls are running at a rate of about 2,900 a day, nearly ten times normal, most from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay. The Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center is at maximum capacity with mutual aid from San Patricio and Bee counties. Call 911 only if someone is in immediate danger; give your address first, then how many people are with you and whether anyone is hurt. For closures, shelters and power, check the City of Corpus Christi website. The Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway remain closed.

stories.headline: 486 rescued so far, 341 by air: Coast Guard helicopters have not stopped since landfall
stories.dek: Coast Guard crews have flown 180 hoists over Flour Bluff and North Beach. More helicopters are on the way from Houston.
body: Coast Guard helicopters are still over Flour Bluff and North Beach this afternoon, and they have not stopped since Hurricane Rafael came ashore.

Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi says crews from Air Station Corpus Christi have flown rescue operations continuously since 1:22 a.m. Tuesday. As of 3 p.m. Wednesday they have completed 180 hoists, pulling people from rooftops and second-story windows.

The count so far: 341 people rescued by air, by Coast Guard crews working with Texas Department of Public Safety and Customs and Border Protection aircraft. Ground and boat teams have confirmed another 145 rescues. That brings the total to 486.
The Coast Guard says its HH-60 Jayhawk helicopters have flown in winds up to 55 knots to reach survivors. Thermal imaging from the air is helping crews find people in floodwater choked with debris.
More help is coming. Sector Commander Capt. Delia Ostrowski-Han has requested additional helicopters from Air Station Houston, starting Thursday morning.
If you are waiting for rescue:
Stay where you are if it is safe. Go to the highest floor. Do not go into an attic unless there is a way out through the roof.
Signal from a window or the roof with a flashlight or your phone.
Call 911 only if someone is in immediate danger, and give your address first.
Do not walk or drive into floodwater.
The Harbor Bridge and the Nueces Bay Causeway remain closed. Portland and North Beach are cut off from downtown until inspections are finished.
Harborline 6 is reporting from its backup studio and will update this count as the Coast Guard releases new numbers.

stories.headline: Coast Guard helicopters pull hundreds from rooftops as Texas coast counts Rafael's toll
stories.dek: Aircrews have hoisted survivors in Corpus Christi almost without pause since the hurricane's landfall; 486 people had been rescued by Wednesday afternoon.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Coast Guard helicopter crews have been lifting people off rooftops in this flooded port city almost without pause since Hurricane Rafael made landfall, and by Wednesday afternoon rescuers working by air, boat and on foot had reached 486 people, the Coast Guard said.

Crews from Air Station Corpus Christi began flying at 1:22 a.m. Tuesday, minutes after the Category 3 storm came ashore near Port Aransas, and had completed 180 hoists as of 3 p.m. Wednesday, Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi said. In all, 341 people had been rescued by air by Coast Guard, Texas Department of Public Safety and Customs and Border Protection aircraft. Ground and boat teams accounted for another 145.

The helicopters, HH-60 Jayhawks, flew in winds of up to 55 knots to reach survivors on roofs and in second-story windows in Flour Bluff and North Beach, two low-lying communities on Corpus Christi Bay, the Coast Guard said. It said aerial thermal imaging had been instrumental in finding people in debris-filled floodwater.

The sector's commander, Capt. Delia Ostrowski-Han, has asked for more rotary-wing aircraft from Air Station Houston beginning Thursday morning, a sign that officials expect the air operation to continue.

The scale of the flooding became clearer Wednesday. Satellite imagery showed about 43 square miles under water across Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties. Nueces County Emergency Management had confirmed twelve deaths as of Wednesday morning and cautioned that the number could rise as search teams reach more neighborhoods. More than 72,000 utility customers were without power.

Two of the main routes into the city's bayfront, the Harbor Bridge and the Nueces Bay Causeway, remained closed pending inspection, cutting off North Beach and the neighboring city of Portland from downtown and leaving aircraft and boats as the fastest way in.

Emergency dispatchers were taking calls at a rate of about 2,900 a day, nearly ten times normal, most from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay. Officials urged residents to call 911 only for life-threatening emergencies and to stay out of floodwater.

stories.headline: 702 rescued; search teams now going block by block in Greenwood and Molina
stories.dek: If you are still in your home and need help, put something bright in a window or on the roof. Flour Bluff searches are complete.
body: Search and rescue teams have now reached 702 people since Hurricane Rafael hit, and tonight the search is moving into new neighborhoods.
Nueces County Emergency Management says the combined teams had 702 confirmed rescues as of 6 p.m. Thursday. That is up from 486 on Wednesday afternoon.

Where crews are working now: the county says searches have expanded into Districts 3 and 4, where floodwater two to three feet deep is still standing in low-lying neighborhoods. Texas Task Force 1 swift-water teams are running systematic grid searches in the Greenwood and Molina neighborhoods.

In Flour Bluff, Dispatch Chief Elena Vasquez-Okafor of the Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center says all known stranded survivors have been reached. Operations are now focused on Calallen and the northwest mainland.
If you are still in your home and need help:
Place a bright-colored item in a window that can be seen from the street, or on your roof. A towel, a shirt or a sheet will work.
Do not try to walk out through floodwater.
Call 911 if someone is in immediate danger.
If a neighbor left before the storm, tell a search team when they reach your block so they do not spend time on an empty house.
The county also says it has confirmed 23 storm-related deaths as of Thursday evening.
The Harbor Bridge and the Nueces Bay Causeway are still closed, so crews are reaching North Beach and Portland by boat and by air.
Harborline 6 will update the rescue count when the county releases new numbers.

stories.headline: The helicopters came first to the bay. The boats are coming now to the Westside
stories.dek: Two days after Rafael, searches are moving into neighborhoods where the water has not left, and where many people had no way to leave before it came.
body: On Thursday evening the water on some streets in Molina was still above the knee, flat and brown and going nowhere. A woman on a porch there, who asked not to be named because she was worried about her landlord, had tied a yellow bath towel to the railing. She had heard on a neighbor's radio that it was what you were supposed to do.

It is. Nueces County Emergency Management said Thursday that residents who are still in their homes and need help should place a bright-colored item in a visible window or on the roof, and should not try to walk out through floodwater. The county said search teams had made 702 confirmed rescues as of 6 p.m., and that it had confirmed 23 storm-related deaths.

The first two days of this rescue belonged to the helicopters and to the neighborhoods on the bay. By Wednesday afternoon the Coast Guard had counted 341 people rescued by air, most of them from rooftops and upper windows in Flour Bluff and North Beach. Elena Vasquez-Okafor, dispatch chief of the Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center, said Thursday that all known stranded survivors in Flour Bluff have now been reached.

What is left is slower. The county said operations have expanded into Districts 3 and 4, where surge flooding has persisted at depths of two to three feet in low-lying neighborhoods, and that Texas Task Force 1 swift-water units are conducting systematic grid searches in Greenwood and Molina. A grid search means every structure on every block, checked and marked, whether or not anyone called.

That matters in these neighborhoods more than most. Many households on the Westside do not have a car. Before the storm, county emergency managers urged people without transportation to sign up for evacuation rides, and advocates warned that the gaps in that system would leave people behind. People who could not leave are also less likely to have a charged phone two days after the power failed. A search that waits for a call will miss them. A search that goes door to door will not.

Shallow, standing water brings its own danger. It hides open drains and downed lines, and it is too shallow for a helicopter rescue to be the obvious answer and too deep for a child or an older person to walk through. The county's instruction is to stay put, signal and wait.
The woman with the towel said two boats had passed the end of her street before dark. She was going to leave the porch light off, she said, to save the battery in her flashlight, and listen.

stories.headline: 911 by the numbers: 2,900 calls Wednesday, a record 2,109 rescue requests Thursday
stories.dek: The county has released the first full count of emergency calls since Rafael. Volume is expected to stay high for weeks. Here is when to call and when not to.
body: The 911 center that serves Nueces County has just had the two busiest days in its history, and county officials say the pace is not letting up soon.

Nueces County Emergency Management Coordinator Lt. Col. Raymond Okafor-Williams said Friday that the Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center handled about 2,900 emergency calls on Wednesday. That is the busiest day the center has ever had and nearly ten times a normal day.

Thursday set a different record: 2,109 rescue requests, the most the center has taken in a single day. Okafor-Williams said that surge came mainly from residents trapped by floodwater in Districts 3 and 4.
On Tuesday, the day Rafael made landfall, the center took about 1,840 calls. About 1,100 of them were rescue-related.
Add it up and the center handled more than 7,300 calls in the first three days. A normal three-day stretch is fewer than 1,000.
"Our dispatchers and the swift water rescue teams from Texas Task Force 1 worked through the night and into the next day to reach everyone who called," Okafor-Williams said.
Dispatchers from San Patricio and Bee counties are still helping answer calls. The county expects call volume to stay elevated for several weeks as recovery work continues.
What you need to know:
Call 911 if someone is in immediate danger. Give your location first.
Do not call 911 for road closures, shelter locations or power questions. Check the City of Corpus Christi website, or call 211 for shelter information.
If you called for help earlier and no longer need it, tell a dispatcher or a responder so crews are not sent to an empty house.
Do not walk or drive into floodwater.

stories.headline: Texas 911 center logs busiest days on record after Hurricane Rafael, leans on neighboring counties
stories.dek: The dispatch hub for Corpus Christi took about 2,900 calls in one day and a record 2,109 rescue requests the next, officials said, with help from two nearby counties.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — The emergency dispatch center for the Corpus Christi area handled more calls in the three days after Hurricane Rafael than it normally takes in three weeks, county officials said Friday, offering the first full measure of the strain the storm put on the region's 911 system.

The Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center took about 2,900 emergency calls on Wednesday, the day after landfall, said Lt. Col. Raymond Okafor-Williams, emergency management coordinator for Nueces County. He called it the busiest day in the center's history and nearly ten times a normal day. On Thursday the center processed 2,109 requests for rescue, the most it has received in a single day.

In all, the center handled more than 7,300 calls over the first three days of the response, compared with fewer than 1,000 in a normal three-day period, Okafor-Williams said. About 1,840 calls came in on Tuesday, the day of landfall, about 1,100 of them related to rescues.
The rescue requests on Thursday came mainly from residents trapped by floodwater in two of the city's water districts, he said, as crews worked into neighborhoods where the surge had not drained.

The center has kept up by borrowing people. Dispatchers from neighboring San Patricio and Bee counties have been answering calls alongside local staff since the storm arrived, an arrangement known as mutual aid that is common in disasters but rarely sustained at this scale for a mid-sized city. Officials said that support will continue and that they expect call volume to stay high for several weeks.

"Our dispatchers and the swift water rescue teams from Texas Task Force 1 worked through the night and into the next day to reach everyone who called," Okafor-Williams said. "We are proud of the professionalism shown by every member of the CBECC team."

Rafael came ashore near Port Aransas early Tuesday as a Category 3 hurricane. Search and rescue teams had recorded 702 rescues as of Thursday evening, and the county has confirmed 23 storm-related deaths.

stories.headline: FEMA drone survey: 4,200 to 5,800 structures with major or severe damage in Nueces County
stories.dek: Eight survey drones flew residential and coastal areas Friday and Saturday. The numbers are preliminary. Here is what the survey does and does not mean for your home.
body: FEMA has its first count of what Hurricane Rafael did to buildings in Nueces County. The agency says between 4,200 and 5,800 structures have major or severe damage, based on a drone survey of residential and coastal areas flown Friday and Saturday.

The numbers are preliminary. FEMA Region 6 says a team of eight unmanned aircraft operated by a contractor, Argus Aerial Systems, covered 180 square kilometers and that the estimate comes from automated analysis of about 847,000 image tiles. The agency says the figures will be updated as the survey expands to other areas, including the utility corridor and commercial districts.

"The aerial survey gives us the most comprehensive picture we have had in the first days after a Gulf Coast hurricane," FEMA Federal Coordinating Officer Dennis Park said. He said the results are going directly to Nueces County emergency management and the City of Corpus Christi to help decide where crews and supplies go.
What this means for you:
The survey is not an inspection of your home, and it does not decide what help you get. FEMA has not released a list of addresses.
If you saw small aircraft flying a grid over your neighborhood Friday or Saturday, that was the survey. More flights are scheduled within the week over utility sites and the port.
Keep documenting your own damage. Take photos and video of every room and the outside of the building before you clean up, and keep receipts.

The federal disaster declaration so far covers debris removal and emergency work. FEMA says help for households has not been approved, and there is nothing to register for yet. No one should charge you a fee to get on a list.
A citywide boil-water notice took effect Saturday morning. Bring water to a rolling boil for two minutes before you drink it or cook with it.
Harborline 6 will update this story when FEMA releases revised figures.

stories.headline: Los drones que vio sobre su barrio eran de FEMA: primer conteo de daños / The drones over your neighborhood were FEMA's: first damage count
stories.dek: FEMA calcula entre 4,200 y 5,800 estructuras con daños mayores o severos en el condado de Nueces. Las cifras son preliminares. / FEMA estimates 4,200 to 5,800 structures with major or severe damage; the figures are preliminary.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas — Muchos oyentes nos llamaron el viernes y el sábado para preguntar por unos aviones pequeños que volaban en línea recta, ida y vuelta, sobre sus casas. Ya tenemos la respuesta: eran drones de FEMA que tomaban fotos de los daños que dejó el huracán Rafael.

La Región 6 de FEMA informó este sábado que un equipo de ocho aeronaves no tripuladas, operadas por la empresa contratista Argus Aerial Systems, cubrió 180 kilómetros cuadrados de zonas residenciales y costeras entre el 17 y el 18 de septiembre. Con esas imágenes, la agencia calcula que entre 4,200 y 5,800 estructuras del condado de Nueces sufrieron daños mayores o severos.

Son cifras preliminares. FEMA dice que las va a actualizar cuando el estudio llegue a otras zonas, entre ellas las instalaciones de servicios públicos y los distritos comerciales. Los resultados se están compartiendo con la oficina de manejo de emergencias del condado y con la ciudad para decidir a dónde mandar cuadrillas y suministros.

Lo que usted debe saber: el estudio no es una inspección de su casa y no decide qué ayuda recibirá. FEMA no ha publicado una lista de direcciones. Siga tomando fotos y video de sus daños antes de limpiar, y guarde sus recibos.

También recuerde que la declaración federal de desastre cubre, por ahora, la limpieza de escombros y los trabajos de emergencia. La ayuda directa para familias todavía no está aprobada y no hay ninguna inscripción abierta. Nadie debe cobrarle por apuntarlo en una lista.
Y desde esta mañana hay un aviso de hervir el agua en toda la ciudad: hierva el agua a borbotones durante dos minutos antes de beberla o cocinar.

In English: The small aircraft many listeners saw flying back and forth over their neighborhoods Friday and Saturday were FEMA survey drones. FEMA Region 6 said eight unmanned aircraft operated by Argus Aerial Systems covered 180 square kilometers and that between 4,200 and 5,800 structures in Nueces County have major or severe damage. The figures are preliminary. The survey is not an inspection of your home and does not decide what aid you receive; household aid has not been approved and there is nothing to register for yet. A citywide boil-water notice is in effect: boil water for two minutes.

stories.headline: A machine counted the damaged houses. What the first Rafael survey can tell us, and what it can't
stories.dek: FEMA's estimate of 4,200 to 5,800 badly damaged structures comes from software reading drone photos. The range is wide for a reason.
body: From a few hundred feet up, a house that lost its roof and a house that kept it are easy to tell apart. A house that kept its roof and took four feet of water is not. That difference sits inside the number FEMA released Saturday, and it is worth understanding before the number hardens into fact.

FEMA Region 6 said between 4,200 and 5,800 structures in Nueces County sustained major or severe damage from Hurricane Rafael. The estimate is based on what the agency called the first systematic aerial drone survey of the Corpus Christi metropolitan area: eight unmanned aircraft, operated under contract by Argus Aerial Systems, covering 180 square kilometers of residential and coastal zones on Friday and Saturday. The count was produced by automated analysis of about 847,000 image tiles.

Start with the range. A gap of 1,600 between the low and high figures is the survey being honest about itself. Software sorts each building into a damage class by what the camera sees: missing roof sections, collapsed walls, debris lines, standing water. Where the picture is ambiguous, the building can fall on either side of a line. FEMA called the figures preliminary and said they will be updated as the survey expands, including to the utility corridor and commercial districts.

Then consider what a camera pointed down cannot see. Surge damage happens low and inside: soaked drywall, ruined wiring, a failed foundation under an intact roof. The neighborhoods that flooded deepest are near the bay and the ship channel, and many of the homes there are older, smaller and rented. If water damage is undercounted anywhere, it is most likely to be undercounted there.

That matters because of how the numbers will be used. FEMA Federal Coordinating Officer Dennis Park said the results are being shared with Nueces County emergency management and the City of Corpus Christi "to inform resource deployment." A map that shows heavy damage draws crews, tarps and inspectors. A map that shows less draws less.

None of this makes the survey wrong. It makes it a first pass. FEMA has said that whether households get direct federal help depends on joint damage assessments, and those involve people walking through homes. For residents, the practical advice is unchanged: photograph the damage inside as well as outside, especially the water line, before cleaning up.

stories.headline: Mass rescue ends after five days and 1,427 people; welfare checks begin
stories.dek: County and Coast Guard officials say every known call for rescue has been answered. Residents who have not been contacted by a welfare team should call 211.
body: The boats and helicopters that have worked the flooded neighborhoods of Corpus Christi since Hurricane Rafael made landfall are standing down. Officials said Sunday that mass rescue operations have concluded after five days, with 1,427 confirmed rescues.

The announcement came from Elena Vasquez-Okafor, dispatch chief of the Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center, and Capt. Delia Ostrowski-Han, commander of Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. They said the operation involved 34 coordinated teams at its peak, drawn from the Coast Guard, Texas Task Force 1, the Corpus Christi Fire Department and the Nueces County Sheriff's search and rescue unit.
It also involved 87 civilian boat operators, people with their own boats who were credentialed by the county to work alongside the official teams.

Ostrowski-Han called it the largest helicopter hoist rescue operation in Corpus Christi history. By Wednesday afternoon, the second day of the response, Coast Guard and partner aircraft had already rescued 341 people by air.

Vasquez-Okafor credited the contracted drone operators whose thermal cameras found people in the dark and in debris. "That capability let us put a boat on a specific roof instead of searching a whole block," she said. "It is the difference between minutes and hours."

The end of the rescue phase is not the end of the search. Officials said the remaining teams will shift to welfare checks, going to homes where no one has yet been contacted. Residents who have not been reached by a welfare check team, or who are worried about a neighbor or relative, should call 211.
Search teams recovered two bodies during the operation, both from a submerged vehicle on Violet Road. The county's confirmed storm death toll stands at 23.

The count rose quickly through the week: 486 by Wednesday afternoon, 702 by Thursday evening, 1,427 by Sunday. The steepest climb came after teams moved inland from the bayfront into neighborhoods where the water stayed for days.
The city remains under a boil-water notice issued Saturday, and officials asked residents returning to flooded homes to photograph damage before cleaning up and to stay out of standing water.

stories.headline: Termina el rescate masivo con 1,427 personas a salvo; si nadie ha pasado por su casa, llame al 2-1-1 / Mass rescue ends with 1,427 people saved; if no one has checked on you, call 2-1-1
stories.dek: Los equipos ahora van casa por casa para verificar que la gente esté bien. / Teams are now going door to door on welfare checks.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas — Después de cinco días, las autoridades dieron por terminadas este domingo las operaciones de rescate masivo por el huracán Rafael. En total, 1,427 personas fueron rescatadas, informaron el Centro de Comunicaciones de Emergencia del Coastal Bend y la Guardia Costera.

En el momento de mayor actividad trabajaron 34 equipos coordinados: la Guardia Costera, el equipo Texas Task Force 1, los bomberos de Corpus Christi y la unidad de búsqueda y rescate del alguacil del condado de Nueces. También ayudaron 87 dueños de lanchas particulares, acreditados por el condado. La comandante del sector de la Guardia Costera, la capitana Delia Ostrowski-Han, dijo que fue la operación de rescate con helicóptero más grande en la historia de Corpus Christi.
Que termine el rescate masivo no quiere decir que se acabó la búsqueda. Los equipos que quedan van a pasar casa por casa para verificar que las personas estén bien.

Lo más importante para nuestros oyentes: si ningún equipo ha pasado por su casa, o si usted no ha podido comunicarse con un familiar o un vecino, llame al 2-1-1. La línea atiende en español. Diga la dirección y cuántas personas viven ahí. Si hay una emergencia en este momento, llame al 9-1-1.
Los equipos recuperaron dos cuerpos durante la operación, los dos en un vehículo sumergido en Violet Road. El condado ha confirmado 23 muertes por la tormenta.

Si usted regresa a una casa inundada, tome fotos de los daños antes de limpiar, por dentro y por fuera, y no camine por agua estancada. Recuerde que el aviso de hervir el agua sigue vigente en toda la ciudad: hiérvala durante dos minutos.
En KNCB queremos dar las gracias a los vecinos que salieron con sus propias lanchas.

In English: Officials said Sunday that mass rescue operations have ended after five days, with 1,427 people rescued. Thirty-four teams worked at the peak, along with 87 credentialed civilian boat operators; the Coast Guard called it the largest helicopter hoist rescue operation in Corpus Christi history. Teams are now making door-to-door welfare checks. If no one has checked on your home, or you cannot reach a relative or neighbor, call 2-1-1, which answers in Spanish. The county has confirmed 23 storm deaths. The citywide boil-water notice remains in effect: boil water for two minutes.

stories.headline: Coast Guard files Rafael SAR summary: 341 hoists, 1,041 surface rescues; after-action review due in 90 days
stories.dek: Sector Corpus Christi's incident summary report certifies 1,427 rescues and credits contracted drone operators with 112 thermal annotations used by surface craft.
body: Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi has filed its formal Incident Summary Report for the Hurricane Rafael search and rescue operation with Coast Guard District 8, the sector said Tuesday. The report, ISR-2027-CC-004, certifies 1,427 total rescues.

Breakdown as certified: 341 by helicopter hoist; 1,041 by surface vessel, a category that covers Coast Guard, state and civilian craft; and 45 ambulatory survivor contacts, meaning people who were found and assisted but did not need to be lifted or carried out.

The surface figure is the one of interest to the working waterfront. Nearly three of every four rescues were made from the water, in flooded streets and along the bay shore, not from the air. County officials said Sunday that 87 credentialed civilian boat operators worked alongside the official teams, and that 34 teams were coordinated at the peak of the operation.

The report also notes that contracted unmanned aircraft operators provided 112 thermal imaging annotations that were used directly to coordinate surface rescues. In practice that means a marked position passed from an aircraft to a boat crew.

Timeline from Coast Guard and county statements: helicopter operations began at 1:22 a.m. Tuesday, Sept. 14. By 3 p.m. Wednesday, Sept. 15, crews had completed 180 hoists and all rescues by air stood at 341, with 486 people reached in total. The cumulative count was 702 on Thursday evening and 1,427 when mass rescue operations concluded Sunday, Sept. 19.

Channel status is unchanged. The Corpus Christi Ship Channel has been closed to all traffic since Port Condition Zulu was set at noon on Monday, Sept. 13, and remains closed for damage surveys and for the oil spill response in the Inner Harbor. Rescue craft operated inside the bays under Coast Guard direction; no commercial movements have resumed.

A formal after-action review of the SAR operation will be conducted within 90 days, the Coast Guard said. For operators, the items to watch in that review are how civilian vessels were credentialed and tasked, how positions were passed between aircraft, drones and boats, and whether those arrangements are written into the area's contingency plans before next season.
The Coast Guard thanked the community and its mutual-aid partners for their response.

stories.headline: Most of Rafael's rescues came by boat. Many of the boats belonged to the neighbors
stories.dek: The Coast Guard's final count credits surface craft with 1,041 of 1,427 rescues. Eighty-seven of the people at the helm were civilians.
body: The pictures people will remember from Hurricane Rafael are of helicopters: an orange-and-white Jayhawk holding steady over a roof in Flour Bluff, a rescue swimmer going down the wire. The numbers the Coast Guard filed Tuesday tell a somewhat different story. Most of the people who were rescued left by boat.

Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi said it has submitted its formal summary of the search and rescue operation to Coast Guard District 8. The report certifies 1,427 rescues: 341 by helicopter hoist, 1,041 by surface vessel and 45 ambulatory survivor contacts. The surface count includes Coast Guard, state and civilian craft.

The civilians were not an afterthought. When officials announced the end of mass rescue operations on Sunday, they said 87 credentialed civilian boat operators had worked alongside 34 coordinated teams from the Coast Guard, Texas Task Force 1, the Corpus Christi Fire Department and the Nueces County Sheriff's search and rescue unit.

Credentialed is the important word. In the military and in the Coast Guard, an operation works because everyone in it is known to whoever is running it: who they are, what they are driving, where they have been sent. A volunteer in a bay boat becomes useful to a rescue the moment a dispatcher can give that boat an address and hear back what was found. Without that, the boat is one more thing in the water to keep track of.

The same idea shows up in a line of the report about drones. Contracted unmanned aircraft operators provided 112 thermal imaging annotations that were used directly to coordinate surface rescues, the Coast Guard said. A camera in the air found a warm shape on a roof or in the water; someone marked it; a boat went to the mark.

The helicopters did what only helicopters can do. In the first day and a half, when the wind was still blowing up to 55 knots and the water in the bayside neighborhoods was too rough and too full of debris for small boats, aircrews made 180 hoists and aircraft accounted for all 341 of the rescues by air that the final report certifies. The boats took over as the water calmed and the search moved inland.

The Coast Guard said a formal after-action review will be conducted within 90 days. For military families at the air station who watched crews fly around the clock last week, and for the neighbors who launched from flooded streets, that review is where the lesson of the two numbers, 341 and 1,041, gets written down.

stories.headline: Dispatch center confirms 23 unfounded emergency calls from prepaid phones; matter referred to law enforcement
stories.dek: The calls, first reported by Coastline Public Radio, sent responders to addresses near two utility sites where no one needed help. The center will not say who it thinks made them.
body: Twenty-three times since Sept. 21, someone called for help in Corpus Christi and there was no one to help when responders arrived. The Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center confirmed the pattern Friday and said it has passed what it knows to law enforcement.

The calls were first reported Friday by Coastline Public Radio, which obtained dispatch records through a public records request. According to those records, 23 calls from unregistered prepaid phones reported emergencies at addresses in northwest and central Corpus Christi near two utility sites. At least eleven described trapped residents. Responders found no one and no emergency at any of the locations.

Dispatch Chief Elena Vasquez-Okafor confirmed the unfounded calls. She said the center had flagged the cluster internally and referred the information to its law enforcement partners. No suspects have been identified.

Vasquez-Okafor declined to say whether the center believes the calls were connected to one another or why they were concentrated near utility sites. "What I can describe is the pattern: prepaid phones, addresses that did not check out, and no one there when our units arrived," she said. "What it means is a question for investigators, and I am not going to get ahead of them."

The center did not name the utility sites, and the records described by Coastline do not say which agencies are reviewing them. The Ledger has filed its own request for the call records, including the times of the calls and the units sent.

The cost of a false call is measured in crews. Each report of a trapped resident draws a response that cannot be somewhere else at the same time, and it comes while the center is still running far above its normal load. County officials said a week ago that the center had handled more than 7,300 calls in the first three days after Hurricane Rafael, and that they expected volume to stay elevated for weeks.

Making a false report to 911 is a crime under Texas law. Anyone with information about the calls can contact the Corpus Christi Police Department or the Nueces County Sheriff's Office. Residents who do need help should not hesitate to call; dispatchers are sending units to every report.

stories.headline: New number for boil-water questions: call the NuecesInfoLine, not 911
stories.dek: The county opened an information line Sunday night after the boil-water notice for Districts 3 and 4 sent a wave of calls to 911.
body: There is a new number to call tonight if you have questions about the boil-water notice for Districts 3 and 4. It is the NuecesInfoLine: 361-826-INFO.
The Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center opened the line Sunday evening. The center says it is seeing a significant increase in calls tied to the notice, which went out at 5:30 p.m.
"911 is for life-threatening emergencies only," Director Patricia Escamilla-Voss says. "Please use that number and keep 911 available for people whose lives are in danger."
What the NuecesInfoLine can tell you: what the boil-water notice means, where the water distribution sites are, and when water service is expected to be restored.
The line is staffed 24 hours a day, seven days a week. For Spanish, press 2.
Water distribution sites are open at:
Tuloso-Midway High School gym
Woodlawn Community Center
Cefe Valenzuela Park
Hours and addresses are on the City of Corpus Christi emergency management website.

Who is under the new notice: about 48,000 residents in Water Districts 3 and 4, which cover ZIP codes 78401, 78405, 78407, 78408, 78416 and 78417. The citywide boil-water notice issued Sept. 18 also remains in effect for everyone else.
What to do: bring water to a rolling boil for two minutes before you drink it, cook with it, make ice or brush your teeth. Let it cool before using it. Bottled water is fine.
Call 911 only if someone is in immediate danger.
Harborline 6 will update this story as the city releases more information.

stories.headline: Para preguntas sobre el agua, marque la NuecesInfoLine y oprima el 2 / For water questions, call the NuecesInfoLine and press 2
stories.dek: La línea 361-826-INFO atiende en español las 24 horas. El 9-1-1 es solo para emergencias de vida o muerte. / The 361-826-INFO line answers in Spanish around the clock; 911 is only for life-threatening emergencies.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas — Si usted vive en los Distritos de Agua 3 y 4 y tiene preguntas sobre el aviso de hervir el agua, hay un número para eso, y no es el 9-1-1. Es la NuecesInfoLine: 361-826-INFO. Para español, oprima el 2.

El Centro de Comunicaciones de Emergencia del Coastal Bend abrió la línea el domingo por la noche, después de que el aviso para los dos distritos provocó un aumento importante de llamadas al 9-1-1. "El 9-1-1 es solo para emergencias que ponen en peligro la vida", dijo la directora del centro, Patricia Escamilla-Voss, en declaraciones traducidas por KNCB. Pidió usar la nueva línea y dejar el 9-1-1 libre para las personas cuya vida está en peligro.
La línea funciona las 24 horas. Los operadores pueden explicarle el aviso, decirle dónde se reparte agua y cuándo se espera que vuelva el servicio normal.

Esto es importante para nuestra comunidad por una razón que usted ya conoce. El aviso para los Distritos 3 y 4 salió en inglés el domingo a las 5:30 de la tarde. La versión oficial en español llegó a KNCB a las 6:03 de la mañana de este lunes, más de 12 horas después, y la pusimos al aire en ese momento. Si anoche usted no supo qué hacer, no fue su culpa.
Lo que debe hacer ahora: hierva el agua a borbotones durante dos minutos antes de beberla, cocinar, hacer hielo o lavarse los dientes. Déjela enfriar. El agua embotellada es segura.
A quién le toca: a unos 48,000 residentes de los códigos postales 78401, 78405, 78407, 78408, 78416 y 78417. El aviso para toda la ciudad, del 18 de septiembre, sigue vigente para los demás.
Dónde hay agua: en el gimnasio de la preparatoria Tuloso-Midway, en el Centro Comunitario Woodlawn y en el parque Cefe Valenzuela.

In English: For questions about the boil-water notice in Water Districts 3 and 4, call the NuecesInfoLine at 361-826-INFO and press 2 for Spanish; it is staffed around the clock. Keep 911 for life-threatening emergencies. The English notice went out Sunday at 5:30 p.m.; the official Spanish version reached KNCB at 6:03 a.m. Monday, more than 12 hours later. Boil water for two minutes. Water is available at the Tuloso-Midway High School gym, Woodlawn Community Center and Cefe Valenzuela Park.

stories.headline: Aerial survey of utility sites finds storm damage at 14 of 23; two substations flagged for inspection
stories.dek: FEMA's second survey phase covered substations, the water plant, pump stations and telecom sites. Engineers are being sent back to the Harbor View and Crosstown substations.
body: A federal aerial survey of the Corpus Christi area's utility sites found visible storm damage at 14 of the 23 locations it examined and singled out two electrical substations for a closer look by engineers, according to a summary released Wednesday by FEMA's Mitigation Assessment Team.

The survey, the second phase of FEMA's aerial assessment of Hurricane Rafael, was flown from Thursday, Sept. 23, through Sunday, Sept. 26. It covered five Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority electrical substations, the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant, four pumping stations and nine telecommunications relay facilities, along with other utility sites.

At O.N. Stevens, the plant that supplies the city's drinking water, the summary reports moderate roof damage to the C-pump station. The plant lost both of its power feeds during the storm, and the city has been under a boil-water notice since Sept. 18.

The summary identifies two of the authority's substations, Harbor View and Crosstown, "as requiring follow-up engineering inspection due to equipment configurations observed in the imagery." It does not say what the configurations were or whether they are related to storm damage. The authority said Tuesday that crews were at two facilities investigating protective relay conditions and that it expected the final 32,000 affected customers to be restored within seven to 10 days; it did not name the facilities.

Rafael Montoya-Chen, chief of the Texas Division of Emergency Management's infrastructure division, said the value of the flights is in what they let repair crews do next. "The aerial survey has given engineers a roadmap so that when crews reach those sites, they know what to look for and can prioritize the most critical restoration steps," he said.

The first phase of the survey, released Sept. 18, estimated that between 4,200 and 5,800 structures in Nueces County had major or severe damage. This phase counts no homes. It looks only at the equipment that keeps power, water and communications running.

The full set of Phase 2 images is not public. FEMA said it is available to credentialed government users through the agency's GeoPlatform. The Ledger has asked the authority when the inspections at Harbor View and Crosstown will take place and whether the results will be released.

stories.headline: Federal survey of storm-hit Texas utility sites flags two substations for follow-up
stories.dek: FEMA's aerial assessment after Hurricane Rafael found visible damage at 14 of 23 utility sites and asked for engineering inspections at two substations where outages have dragged on.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — A federal aerial survey of utility infrastructure damaged by Hurricane Rafael has flagged two electrical substations for follow-up inspection by engineers, adding a new question to a power restoration that has already run longer than the local utility first projected.

The Federal Emergency Management Agency's Mitigation Assessment Team said Wednesday that its survey of 23 utility sites in the Corpus Christi area, flown Sept. 23 through Sept. 26, found visible storm damage at 14 of them. The sites included five electrical substations operated by the Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority, the city's main water treatment plant, four pumping stations and nine telecommunications relay facilities.

Two of the substations, known as Harbor View and Crosstown, were identified as needing engineering inspection "due to equipment configurations observed in the imagery," the summary said. It gave no further description. The water plant, which lost power during the storm, had moderate roof damage to one pump station.

The finding lands a day after the utility said publicly that conditions at two of its facilities were slowing the work. The authority said Tuesday that crews were investigating protective relay conditions made worse by storm debris and that the last 32,000 customers without power should be restored within seven to 10 days. It did not identify the facilities, and neither the utility nor FEMA has said whether they are the two named in the survey.

Aerial surveys have become a standard early step after major storms because they can cover ground that crews cannot yet reach. "The aerial survey has given engineers a roadmap so that when crews reach those sites, they know what to look for and can prioritize the most critical restoration steps," said Rafael Montoya-Chen, who heads the infrastructure division of the Texas Division of Emergency Management.

An earlier phase of the same program, released four days after the Sept. 14 landfall, estimated that 4,200 to 5,800 structures in Nueces County had major or severe damage. The detailed utility imagery has not been made public; FEMA said it is available to credentialed government users.

stories.headline: Four weeks, 44,200 calls: the 911 center's long month, and what the record of it could show
stories.dek: Call volume is nearly back to normal and borrowed dispatchers are going home. The center is keeping every call record for its after-action review.
body: For 28 days the phones at the Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center did not ring the way they are supposed to. On Tuesday they almost did. The center took 380 calls, it said Wednesday, close to the 310 it handled on an ordinary day before the storm.

Between those two numbers is the month that followed Hurricane Rafael. Director Patricia Escamilla-Voss said the center handled more than 44,200 calls in the four weeks after landfall, about five times its normal volume. The peak came the day after the storm, at about 2,900 calls. The day after that brought a record 2,109 requests for rescue.

"Our dispatchers have shown extraordinary dedication over the past four weeks," Escamilla-Voss said. "The scale and duration of this response was unprecedented for our center, and I am incredibly proud of every person who answered calls, coordinated rescues, and kept working through the most demanding conditions I have seen in my career."

The center will begin returning to normal staffing over the next two weeks. The dispatchers from San Patricio and Bee counties who have worked alongside local staff since landfall will start scaling back on Thursday.

What stays is the record. Escamilla-Voss said the center is retaining all call records and audio as part of its standard after-action review. That archive is more than paperwork. Every call carries a time, a location and a type of emergency, and together they make a map of the storm drawn by the people who lived it: where the water rose first, where help was asked for most, and how long the asking went on.

It could also answer questions the center has not yet taken up in public. County officials said in September that the record surge in rescue requests came mainly from Districts 3 and 4. Those districts include some of the city's lowest-income neighborhoods, and they are the same ones that have been under a separate boil-water notice since Sept. 26. Whether callers there waited longer, or called more than once before help came, is something the records can show and a summary cannot.
The archive also holds the 23 calls from prepaid phones that sent responders to addresses where no one needed help, a cluster the center has referred to law enforcement.
Coastline Public Radio has requested the after-action review when it is complete.

stories.headline: The storm, photographed 6.2 million times: Rafael aerial archive opens to the public
stories.dek: FEMA has finished its aerial survey of the Corpus Christi area and posted reduced-resolution imagery from the first two phases. Here is what is in it and who can use it.
body: If you want to see what Hurricane Rafael did to your block, you can now look for yourself. FEMA Region 6 said Friday that it has finished its aerial assessment of the storm and, starting the same day, made part of the imagery public.

The program ran from a baseline flown on Sept. 12, two days before landfall, through Oct. 29. In that time federal, state and contracted aircraft produced more than 6.2 million georeferenced image tiles covering 183 square kilometers of the Corpus Christi metropolitan area. FEMA called it the most comprehensive post-storm aerial survey conducted on the Texas Gulf Coast, and said the archive spans every phase of the disaster, from before the storm through the recovery still under way.

What is public is narrower than that. FEMA said downsampled imagery, meaning pictures at reduced resolution, from the Phase 1 and Phase 2 surveys is available through the agency's OpenData portal to academic researchers, local governments and community organizations working on recovery planning. Phase 1 was the residential and coastal survey behind the agency's first estimate, on Sept. 18, of 4,200 to 5,800 structures with major or severe damage. Phase 2, released Sept. 29, covered utility sites. Anyone who needs full-resolution imagery has to ask FEMA Region 6's geospatial office.

"This imagery archive is a resource that will support not just today's recovery, but future preparedness for the entire Texas Gulf Coast," FEMA Federal Coordinating Officer Dennis Park said. He thanked NOAA, the Texas Army National Guard and the agency's contractors for flying the missions.

For neighborhood groups, the before-and-after pairing is the useful part. A baseline image from Sept. 12 next to one from the week after landfall shows which roofs, fences and trees were there before the storm, something that is hard to prove from memory. Tenant advocates and church relief hubs that have spent six weeks helping people document losses can now point to a dated federal photograph.

There are limits. Reduced resolution blurs the detail that matters most in a dispute over a single house, and an aerial picture still cannot see water damage under an intact roof. And the archive records what happened; it does not explain it. It is a record of the damage, open to more people than before.
